Its timbre combines the bright brittleness of percussion with the resonant warmth of a harmonica, produced by the interaction of the vibrating reed and the mouth cavity. Its range is mainly in the low and middle frequencies, and pitch depends on the thickness of the reed and the speed of vibration. Its sound has a marked nasal colour; unlike the crystalline penetration of the Western harmonica it has a warm, slightly hoarse texture. Compared with traditional percussion it has more rhythmic flexibility and control; compared with bamboo instruments its timbre is more inward and mysterious. The instrument's resonance depends mainly on the player's mouth cavity, so that every stroke can show subtle changes of timbre.

This reed instrument is made of bamboo or animal horn, and over several centuries of development it has gradually become indispensable in Bihu music. The craft of making the gogona reflects Assam's rich bamboo resources and handicraft tradition, and the playing technique handed down from generation to generation preserves its original musical aesthetic.

It is made of bamboo or horn with one end forked; the player grips the solid end between the teeth and repeatedly flicks the forked end with a finger to sound it. There are male and female types: the male type is shorter, wider and heavier and can be tucked into a belt or turban; the female type is slimmer and longer and is worn in the hair bun as an ornament when dancing.

This distribution shows that the gogona represents a shared musical heritage of the trans-Himalayan region. Although each people's version differs slightly, its simple construction and distinctive timbre keep it alive in folk music, reflecting cultural exchange and interaction among mountain civilisations.
